card.title: VSEPR shapes read off the steric number

rows.label: Concept
rows.text: Electron pairs around a central atom repel one another and spread as far apart as they can, so counting σ bonds plus lone pairs — the steric number — fixes both the shape and the hybridisation.

figure.caption: Steric number 2, 3 and 4 give linear, trigonal planar and tetrahedral; lone pairs squeeze the angle.

rows.label: Formula
rows.text: SN = σ bonds + lone pairs;  2 → sp, 180°;  3 → sp², 120°;  4 → sp³, 109.5°;  5 → sp³d;  6 → sp³d²

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: Start from a correct Lewis structure, take the repulsion order lone pair–lone pair > lone pair–bond pair > bond pair–bond pair, and apply it to the central atom only.

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: CH₄ 109.5°, NH₃ 107° with one lone pair, H₂O 104.5° with two; CO₂ linear, BF₃ trigonal planar, SF₆ octahedral, XeF₄ square planar.

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: H₂O: 2 σ bonds + 2 lone pairs = steric number 4 → sp³, but the molecular shape is bent and the angle closes to 104.5°.

rows.label: Limitation
rows.text: It is a repulsion model rather than a calculation: transition-metal complexes, d-orbital participation and strongly electronegative substituents break its predictions.

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: Count valence electrons → draw the Lewis structure → σ bonds + lone pairs = SN → electron-pair geometry → remove lone pairs for the molecular shape

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: Lone pairs decide the angle but are never named in the shape: steric number 4 with two lone pairs still reads bent, not tetrahedral.

rows.label: Board question
rows.text: Predict the shape, hybridisation and bond angle of H₂O and NH₃, and explain why they differ from CH₄.
